title: Chapter 46. Of Darkness from Vain Philosophy, and Fabulous Traditions
section: Part IV — Of the Kingdom of Darkness
paragraphs: Philosophy is defined as the knowledge acquired by reasoning—either from the way something is generated to its properties, or from its properties to a possible way of generating that same thing—with the aim of producing, so far as matter and human power allow, the effects that human life requires. So the geometrician, working from the construction of figures, discovers many of their properties, and then from those properties discovers new methods of construction, all by reasoning, in order to measure land and water and serve countless other uses. Likewise the astronomer, working from the rising, setting, and movement of the sun and stars across different parts of the heavens, traces out the causes of day and night and of the changing seasons of the year, and so keeps an account of time. And so it is with the other sciences.

From this definition it is plain that we cannot count as a part of philosophy that original knowledge called experience, in which prudence consists. Experience is not reached by reasoning—it is found in brute animals just as much as in human beings—and is only a memory of how events have followed one another in the past, in which the omission of any small circumstance that alters the outcome frustrates the expectation of even the most prudent person. Reasoning, when done correctly, produces nothing but general, eternal, and unchanging truth.
Nor should we apply the name of philosophy to any false conclusions, since whoever reasons correctly in words he understands can never conclude in an error.
Nor to anything a person knows by supernatural revelation, since that is not reached by reasoning.
Nor to what is gathered by reasoning from the authority of books, since that is not reasoning from cause to effect or from effect to cause; it is not knowledge but faith.

Because the faculty of reasoning follows from the use of speech, it was inevitable that some general truths would have been discovered by reasoning almost as soon as language itself existed. The savages of America are not without good moral sayings; they also have a little arithmetic, enough to add and divide modest numbers—but that does not make them philosophers. Just as plants of grain and grapevines were scattered in small numbers through the fields and woods before human beings recognized their value, made use of them as food, or planted them apart in fields and vineyards (in those days people lived on acorns and drank water), so too there have always been, from the beginning, a few true, general, and useful insights, which are the natural plants of human reason. But they were few at first; people lived on rough experience; there was no method—that is, no sowing or planting of knowledge by itself, separated from the weeds and ordinary growth of error and conjecture. The cause of this was the lack of leisure that follows from having to secure the necessities of life and defend oneself against one's neighbors, and so it could not have been otherwise until great commonwealths were established. Leisure is the mother of philosophy, and the commonwealth is the mother of peace and leisure. Wherever there were first great and flourishing cities, there the study of philosophy first arose. The Gymnosophists of India, the Magi of Persia, and the priests of Chaldea and Egypt are counted the most ancient philosophers, and those countries were the most ancient of kingdoms. Philosophy had not yet appeared among the Greeks and the other peoples of the West, whose commonwealths (perhaps no greater than Lucca or Geneva) never enjoyed peace except when their fears of one another were equal, and had no leisure to observe anything but each other. At length, when war had united many of these smaller Greek cities into fewer and larger ones, seven men from various parts of Greece began to acquire the reputation of being wise—some of them for moral and political sayings, others for the learning of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, which was astronomy and geometry. But we still hear of no schools of philosophy.

After the Athenians, by overthrowing the Persian armies, had gained control of the sea, and through that of all the islands and coastal cities of the Archipelago—both in Asia and Europe—and had grown wealthy, those who had no occupation either at home or abroad had little else to do but, as St. Luke says (Acts 17:21), "tell and hear news," or discourse publicly on philosophy to the young men of the city. Every master took some place for that purpose. Plato used certain public walks called Academia, named after one Academus; Aristotle used the walk of the Temple of Pan, called the Lycaeum; others used the Stoa, the covered walk where merchants' goods were brought ashore; and others used other places, where they spent their leisure time teaching or debating their opinions. Some used any spot where they could gather the city's young people to hear them talk. This was also what Carneades did at Rome when he was an ambassador, which led Cato to advise the Senate to dispatch him quickly, for fear of corrupting the manners of the young men who delighted to hear him say what they took to be fine things.

From this practice came the name Schola for the place where any of them taught and debated, which in their language meant "leisure"; and their debates were called Diatribae, that is, "passing of the time." The philosophers themselves took the names of their sects from these schools: those who followed Plato's doctrine were called Academics; the followers of Aristotle were called Peripatetics, from the walk where he taught; and those whom Zeno taught were called Stoics, from the Stoa—as though we should name people after Moorfields, St. Paul's Church, or the Exchange because they often gather there to prattle and loiter.

Nevertheless people were so taken with this custom that in time it spread across all of Europe and the better part of Africa, so that schools were publicly established and funded for lectures and debates in almost every commonwealth.

There were also schools long ago among the Jews, both before and after the time of our Savior, but they were schools of their Law. Although they were called synagogues—that is, congregations of the people—because the Law was read, expounded, and disputed in them every Sabbath day, they differed from public schools only in name, not in nature. They existed not only in Jerusalem but in every Gentile city where Jews lived. There was such a school at Damascus, into which Paul entered to persecute; there were others at Antioch, Iconium, and Thessalonica, into which he entered to debate; and such was the synagogue of the Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians, and those of Asia—that is, the school of the Libertines and of Jews who were strangers in Jerusalem. It was members of this school who disputed with Saint Stephen.

But what use have these schools been? What science has been acquired today through their readings and debates? Whatever geometry we have—the mother of all natural science—we do not owe to the schools. Plato, the best of the Greek philosophers, forbade entry to his school to anyone not already in some measure a geometer. Many studied that science to the great benefit of humankind, but there is no mention of their schools, no sect of geometers, and they were not at that time called philosophers. The natural philosophy of those schools was more a dream than a science, and was set out in meaningless and empty language—something that cannot be avoided by anyone who tries to teach philosophy without first attaining a serious knowledge of geometry. Nature works by motion, the paths and degrees of which cannot be known without knowledge of the proportions and properties of lines and figures. Their moral philosophy is nothing but a description of their own passions. The standard of conduct, in the absence of civil government, is the law of nature; and within that, the civil law, which determines what is honest and dishonest, what is just and unjust, and in general what is good and evil. But they make the rules of good and bad turn on their own likes and dislikes, with the result that, given so great a diversity of taste, nothing is generally agreed on, and everyone does (so far as he dares) whatever seems good in his own eyes—to the ruin of the commonwealth. Their logic, which should be the method of reasoning, is nothing but tricks of words and devices for puzzling anyone who tries to challenge them. In short, there is nothing so absurd that some of the old philosophers (as Cicero, himself one of them, said) have not maintained. And I believe that scarcely anything can be more absurdly stated in natural philosophy than what is now called Aristotle's Metaphysics, more contrary to government than much of what he says in his Politics, or more ignorant than a great part of his Ethics.

The Jewish school was originally a school of the Law of Moses, who commanded (Deut. 31:10) that at the end of every seventh year, at the Feast of Tabernacles, the Law should be read to all the people so they might hear and learn it. The reading of the Law that was practiced every Sabbath day after the Captivity should therefore have had no other aim than to acquaint the people with the commandments they were to obey and to expound the writings of the prophets to them. But it is clear from the many rebukes given them by our Savior that they corrupted the text of the Law with their false commentaries and empty traditions, and so little understood the prophets that they neither recognized Christ nor the works he did, for which the prophets had prophesied. Through their lectures and debates in their synagogues, they turned the doctrine of their Law into a fanciful kind of philosophy about the incomprehensible nature of God and of spirits, which they assembled out of the empty philosophy and theology of the Greeks, mixed with their own ideas drawn from the more obscure passages of Scripture that could most easily be twisted to their purpose, and from the legendary traditions of their ancestors.

What is now called a university is a joining together and incorporation under a single government of many public schools in one and the same town or city. Within it, the principal schools were established for the three professions—Roman religion, Roman law, and the art of medicine. The study of philosophy has a place there only as a handmaid to the Roman religion; and since the authority of Aristotle is the only one current there, what they study is not properly philosophy (whose nature does not depend on authors) but Aristotelity. As for geometry, until very recent times it had no place at all, since it was useful only for strict truth. And if any person, through the natural quality of his own mind, had attained any degree of skill in it, he was commonly thought a magician and his art diabolical.

Now to descend to the particular tenets of vain philosophy, passed from Aristotle (and from blindness of understanding) into the universities and from there into the Church, I will first consider their principles. There is a certain Philosophia Prima, on which all other philosophy ought to depend, and which consists chiefly in fixing the meanings of the most universal of all names—those limitations being meant to avoid ambiguity and equivocation in reasoning. They are commonly called definitions, such as the definitions of Body, Time, Place, Matter, Form, Essence, Subject, Substance, Accident, Power, Act, Finite, Infinite, Quantity, Quality, Motion, Action, Passion, and various others required to clarify a person's conceptions about the nature and generation of bodies. The explication—that is, the settling of the meaning—of these and similar terms is commonly called in the schools Metaphysics, as being a part of Aristotle's philosophy that bears that title. But in his case the word had another sense: it meant "books written or placed after his natural philosophy." The schools, however, take them as books of supernatural philosophy, since the word Metaphysics will bear both senses. And indeed what is written there is, for the most part, so far from any possibility of being understood, and so contrary to natural reason, that anyone who thinks there is something in it to be understood must necessarily think it supernatural.

From these metaphysics, which are mixed with Scripture to make school divinity, we are told there exist in the world certain essences separated from bodies, which they call Abstract Essences and Substantial Forms. To unravel that jargon requires more than ordinary attention here, and I ask the indulgence of those who are not used to this kind of discussion while I address those who are. The World—by which I mean not only the earth (the love of which marks "worldly men"), but the universe, that is, the whole mass of everything that exists—is corporeal, that is, body, and has the dimensions of magnitude: length, breadth, and depth. Every part of body is likewise body, and has the same dimensions. So every part of the universe is body, and whatever is not body is no part of the universe. And because the universe is everything, whatever is no part of it is nothing, and so is nowhere. It does not follow from this, however, that spirits are nothing, for they have dimensions and so are really bodies—though in ordinary speech the name "body" is given only to those that are visible or palpable, that is, that have some degree of opacity. Spirits they call "incorporeal," a more honorific name, which may with more piety therefore be assigned to God himself, in whom we consider not what attribute best expresses his nature (which is incomprehensible) but what best expresses our desire to honor him.

To see now on what grounds they say there are abstract essences or substantial forms, we should consider what those words properly mean. Words are used to record for ourselves and make plain to others the thoughts and conceptions of our minds. Some words are names of things conceived—the names of all kinds of bodies that act on the senses and leave impressions in the imagination. Others are names of the imaginations themselves, that is, of the ideas or mental images we have of everything we see or remember. Still others are names of names, or of different kinds of speech, such as Universal, Plural, Singular, Negation, True, False, Syllogism, Interrogation, Promise, Covenant—these are the names of certain forms of speech. Others serve to show the consequence or incompatibility of one name with another, as when one says "a man is a body," meaning that the name "body" follows necessarily from the name "man," both being different names of the same thing, namely man. That consequence is signified by coupling them with the word "is." As we use the verb "is," the Latins use est and the Greeks esti through all its forms. Whether all other nations of the world have a word in their languages that corresponds to it, I cannot say; but I am sure they have no need of one, since placing two names in sequence could—if it were the custom (and custom is what gives words their force)—signify their consequence just as well as the words "is," "be," "are," and the like.

And if there were a language with no verb corresponding to est, is, or be, the people who used it would still be every bit as capable of inferring, concluding, and every kind of reasoning as the Greeks and Latins were. But what then would become of these terms—Entity, Essence, Essential, Essentially—that are derived from such a verb, and of many others that depend on these and are commonly applied as we apply them? They are therefore not names of things; they are signs by which we make known that we conceive that one name or attribute follows from another. When we say "a man is a living body," we do not mean that the man is one thing, the living body another, and the "is" or "being" a third. We mean that the man and the living body are the same thing, because the consequence "if he is a man, he is a living body" is a true consequence, signified by the word "is." Therefore, to be a body, to walk, to be speaking, to live, to see, and similar infinitives—along with corporeity, walking, speaking, life, sight, and the like, which mean the same—are names of nothing, as I have explained more fully elsewhere.

But to what end, someone may ask, is such subtlety in a work of this kind, where I claim to deal with nothing but what is necessary for the doctrine of government and obedience? It is to this end: that people may no longer allow themselves to be misled by those who, by this doctrine of separated essences, built on the empty philosophy of Aristotle, would frighten them away from obeying the laws of their country with empty names—as people frighten birds away from the corn with an empty doublet, a hat, and a crooked stick. On this same ground, when someone has died and been buried, they claim that the soul (that is, the life) can move separately from the body and is observed at night around graves. On the same ground, they say that the figure, color, and taste of a piece of bread continue to exist where, on their own account, no bread is. And on the same ground, they say that faith, wisdom, and the other virtues are sometimes infused into a person, sometimes transmitted into him from heaven—as if the virtuous and their virtues could be parted; along with a great many other claims that serve to lessen the dependence of subjects on the sovereign power of their country. For who will work to obey the laws if he expects obedience to be infused or transmitted into him? Who will not obey a priest who claims to be able to produce God, rather than his sovereign—indeed, rather than God himself? Or who, fearing the appearance of departed spirits, will not show great respect to those who can make the holy water said to drive them away? Let this suffice as an example of the errors brought into the Church from the entities and essences of Aristotle, which he may have known to be false philosophy, but wrote as something agreeable to, and supportive of, the religion of his time—fearing the fate of Socrates.

Having once fallen into this error of separated essences, they are necessarily caught up in many other absurdities that follow from it. Since they insist that these forms are real, they are obliged to assign them some place. But because they hold them to be incorporeal, without any dimension of quantity, and everyone knows that place is dimension and can only be filled by what is corporeal, they prop up their credit with a distinction: that the forms are not located anywhere "circumscriptively" but only "definitively." These terms, being mere words and meaningless on this occasion, pass only in Latin, so that their emptiness may be hidden. The circumscription of a thing is nothing but the determining, or defining, of its place, so both terms of the distinction mean the same. And in particular, of the essence of a person—which, they say, is the soul—they affirm that it is all of it in his little finger, and all of it in every other part of his body, however small; and yet no more soul in the whole body than in any one of those parts. Can anyone think God is served by such absurdities? And yet all this must be believed by those who will believe in the existence of an incorporeal soul separated from the body.

And when they are asked to explain how an incorporeal substance can be capable of pain, and be tormented in the fire of Hell or Purgatory, they have nothing at all to answer except that it cannot be known how fire can act upon souls.

Again, since motion is change of place, and incorporeal substances are not capable of place, they are hard pressed to explain how a soul can leave from here, without the body, to Heaven, Hell, or Purgatory; or how the apparitions of the departed (and, I may add, of the clothes in which they appear) can be observed at night around churches, churchyards, and other places of burial. To this I do not know what they can answer, unless they will say that the figures move "definitively" rather than "circumscriptively," or "spiritually" rather than "temporally"—since such fine-sounding distinctions are equally applicable to any difficulty whatsoever.

As for the meaning of eternity, they will not have it be an endless succession of time, since then they would not be able to give any reason why God's will and his preordaining of things to come should not come before his foreknowledge of those same things, as the efficient cause comes before the effect, or the agent before the action—nor account for many of their other bold opinions about the incomprehensible nature of God. So instead they will teach us that eternity is the standing still of the present time, a Nunc-stans (as the schools call it), which neither they nor anyone else understands—any more than they would a Hic-stans for an infinite greatness of place.

And whereas people divide a body in their thought by counting its parts, and in counting those parts also count the parts of the place it occupies, it cannot help being the case that, in making many parts, we also make many places for those parts. As a result, no human mind can conceive more or fewer parts than there are places for them. Yet they will have us believe that, by the almighty power of God, one body may be at one and the same time in many places, and many bodies at one and the same time in one place—as though it were a tribute to divine power to say that what is, is not; or that what has been, has not been. And these are only a small portion of the absurdities they are driven to, from disputing philosophically about the divine and incomprehensible nature instead of admiring and adoring it; for the attributes we apply to God cannot signify what he is, but ought to signify our desire to honor him with the best names we can think of. Those who venture to reason about his nature from these attributes of honor lose their understanding at the very first attempt, and fall from one absurdity into another, without end and without number—in the same way that a man unfamiliar with court ceremony, on coming into the presence of someone greater than he is used to addressing, stumbles at his entrance, and, to save himself from falling, lets his cloak slip; in trying to recover the cloak he drops his hat; and with one mishap after another reveals his bewilderment and lack of polish.

Now for physics—that is, the knowledge of the subordinate, secondary causes of natural events—they offer nothing but empty words. If you want to know why some kinds of bodies naturally sink toward the earth, and others naturally rise from it, the schools will tell you, out of Aristotle, that the bodies that sink are heavy, and that this heaviness is what causes them to descend. But if you ask what they mean by heaviness, they will define it as an endeavor to go to the center of the earth—so the cause why things sink is an endeavor to be below, which amounts to saying that bodies fall or rise because they do. Or they will tell you that the center of the earth is the place of rest and preservation for heavy things, and that is why they endeavor to be there—as if stones and metals had a desire, or could perceive the place they wanted to be in, the way a human does; or loved rest, the way a human does not; or as if a piece of glass were less safe in the window than falling into the street.

If we want to know why the same body sometimes seems larger (without anything being added to it) than at other times, they say that when it seems smaller it has been condensed; when larger, rarefied. What does condensed and rarefied mean? Condensed, when there is in the same matter less quantity than before; rarefied, when more. As if there could be matter that had no determinate quantity at all, when quantity is nothing else than the determination of matter—that is, of body, by which we say one body is greater or smaller than another by such and such an amount. Or as if a body were made without any quantity at all, and that more or less were afterwards put into it, depending on how dense the body was supposed to be.
As for the cause of the human soul, they say Creatur Infundendo, and Creando Infunditur—that is, "it is created by being infused," and "infused by being created."

For the cause of sense, they offer the ubiquity of species, that is, of the shows or appearances of objects, which when they appear to the eye is sight; when to the ear, hearing; to the palate, taste; to the nostril, smell; and to the rest of the body, feeling.

For the cause of the will to perform any particular action, called Volitio, they assign the Faculty—that is, the general capacity people have to will sometimes one thing, sometimes another, which is called Voluntas—making the power the cause of the act. As if one should give as the cause of people's good or evil acts their ability to do them.

And on many occasions they offer as a cause of natural events their own ignorance, disguised in other words: as when they say that Fortune is the cause of contingent things—that is, of things they know no cause for; or when they attribute many effects to occult qualities, that is, to qualities they do not know about (and therefore, they suppose, that no one else knows about); or to Sympathy, Antipathy, Antiperistasis, Specific Qualities, and other such terms, which signify neither the agent that produces them nor the operation by which they are produced.
If such metaphysics and physics as these are not empty philosophy, then there never was such a thing—and St. Paul would have had no reason to warn us to avoid it.

And for their moral and civil philosophy, it has the same or greater absurdities. If a person performs an unjust action—that is, an action contrary to the Law—God, they say, is the prime cause of the Law, and also the prime cause of that action and all other actions; but no cause at all of the injustice, which is the nonconformity of the action with the Law. This is vain philosophy. You might as well say that one person makes both a straight line and a crooked one, and another makes their incongruity. Such is the philosophy of all those who settle their conclusions before they know their premises, claiming to comprehend what is incomprehensible, and turning attributes of honor into attributes of nature. This is the distinction made to maintain the doctrine of free will, that is, of a human will not subject to the will of God.

Aristotle and other heathen philosophers define good and evil by the appetite of people—and well enough, so long as we are considering them each governed by his own law. For in the condition of those who have no other law but their own appetites, there can be no general rule of good and evil actions. But in a commonwealth this measure is false. The measure is not the appetite of private persons but the Law, which is the will and appetite of the state. And yet this doctrine is still in practice: people judge the goodness or wickedness of their own actions, of others' actions, and even of the actions of the commonwealth itself, by their own passions, and no one calls anything good or evil except what is so in his own eyes, with no regard at all to the public laws—except for monks and friars, who are bound by vow to that simple obedience to their superior which every subject ought to think himself bound by the law of nature to render to the civil sovereign. This private measure of good is a doctrine that is not only vain but also pernicious to the public state.

It is also vain and false philosophy to say that married life is at odds with chastity or continence, and so to treat them as moral vices—as is done by those who argue from chastity and continence as the basis for denying marriage to the clergy. They themselves admit it is no more than a regulation of the Church, requiring of those in holy orders who continually attend the altar and administer the Eucharist a continual abstinence under the name of perpetual chastity, continence, and purity. They therefore characterize married life as a falling-short of chastity and continence, and so make marriage a sin, or at any rate something so impure as to render a man unfit for the altar. If this rule were established because married life is incontinence and contrary to chastity, then all marriage is vice; and if because it is something too impure for a man consecrated to God, then how much more should other natural, necessary, and daily activities that all people perform render them unworthy to be priests, since they are still less clean.

But the underlying foundation of this prohibition is not likely to have been laid on something so flimsy as such errors in moral philosophy, nor on a preference for the single life over married life—which came from the wisdom of St. Paul, who saw how inconvenient it was, for those who in those times of persecution were preachers of the Gospel and forced to flee from one country to another, to be encumbered with the care of a household. Rather it rested on the design of the popes and priests of later times, to make themselves the Clergy, that is, the sole heirs of the Kingdom of God in this world. To make that claim plausible, it became necessary to take from them the institution of marriage, because our Savior says that at the coming of his Kingdom the children of God shall "neither marry, nor be given in marriage, but shall be as the angels in heaven"—that is to say, spiritual. Since they had taken on themselves the name of spiritual, to have allowed themselves married life (when there was no need) would have been an incongruity.

From Aristotle's civil philosophy they have learned to call every form of commonwealth other than the popular one (such as Athens was at that time) a tyranny. All kings they called tyrants; and the aristocracy of the thirty governors set up there by the Lacedaemonians who subdued them, the Thirty Tyrants. They have likewise learned to call the condition of the people under democracy liberty. A tyrant originally meant nothing more than a monarch; but when, in most parts of Greece, that kind of government was afterwards abolished, the name began to signify not only what it did before, but also the hatred which the popular states bore toward it. The name of king also became odious after the deposing of the kings of Rome, since it is natural to all people to suppose that some great fault is being signified by any title used in spite, and against a great enemy. And when the same people become displeased with those who administer a democracy or aristocracy, they have no trouble finding disgraceful names to express their anger: they readily call the one Anarchy and the other Oligarchy, or the Tyranny of a Few. What offends the people is nothing other than the fact that they are governed not as each of them would govern himself, but as the public representative—whether one man or an assembly of men—thinks fit; that is, by an arbitrary government, for which they give bad names to their superiors, never realizing (until perhaps a little after a civil war) that without such arbitrary government, such war must be perpetual; and that it is men and arms, not words and promises, that give the force and power of the laws.

This is therefore another error of Aristotle's Politics: that in a well-ordered commonwealth not men but the laws should govern. What person with his natural senses, even if he can neither read nor write, does not find himself governed by those he fears, and believes can kill or hurt him if he disobeys? Or believes the Law can hurt him—that is, words and paper without the hands and swords of people? This is among the pernicious errors, for it leads people, as often as they dislike their governors, to side with those who call those governors tyrants, and to think it lawful to make war against them. And yet these doctrines are often cherished from the pulpit by the clergy.

There is another error in their civil philosophy (which they never learned from Aristotle, nor from Cicero, nor any other of the heathen): to extend the power of the Law, which is the rule of actions only, to the very thoughts and consciences of people, by examination and inquisition of what they hold, despite the conformity of their speech and actions. By this means people are either punished for answering the truth of their thoughts, or forced to answer an untruth out of fear of punishment. It is true that a civil magistrate, intending to employ a minister in the role of teaching, may inquire whether he is content to preach such and such doctrines, and refuse him the post if he declines. But to compel him to accuse himself of opinions, when his actions are not forbidden by law, is against the law of nature—especially when those who do the compelling are the very same people who teach that one will be damned to eternal and extreme torments if he dies holding a false opinion about an article of the Christian faith. For who, knowing such great danger lies in an error, would not, when natural self-concern obliges him not to risk his soul on his own judgment, prefer his own judgment over that of any other person who has no stake in his damnation?

For a private person, without the authority of the commonwealth—that is, without permission from its representative—to interpret the Law by his own spirit, is another error in politics; but not one drawn from Aristotle or from any other of the heathen philosophers. For none of them denied that within the power of making laws is also included the power of explaining them when need arises. And are not the Scriptures, in all places where they are law, made law by the authority of the commonwealth, and consequently a part of the civil law?

Of the same kind it is when anyone but the sovereign restrains in a person a power that the commonwealth has not restrained—as those do who reserve the preaching of the Gospel to a single order of men, where the laws have left it free. If the state gives me leave to preach or teach—that is, if it does not forbid me—no one can forbid me. If I find myself among the idolaters of America, am I, being a Christian, even though not in holy orders, to think it a sin to preach Jesus Christ until I have received orders from Rome? Or, when I have preached, shall I not answer their doubts and explain the Scriptures to them—that is, shall I not teach? Someone may say that for this, as also for administering the sacraments to them, the necessity shall be regarded as a sufficient mission, which is true. But it is also true that wherever a dispensation is owed because of necessity, no dispensation is needed where there is no law forbidding the act. To deny these functions to those whom the civil sovereign has not denied them is therefore to take away a lawful liberty, which is contrary to the doctrine of civil government.

More examples of vain philosophy brought into religion by the doctors of school-divinity might be produced, but others can notice them for themselves if they please. I will only add this: that the writings of the schoolmen are for the most part nothing but meaningless strings of strange and barbarous words, or of words used in ways foreign to the common usage of the Latin tongue—such as would puzzle Cicero, Varro, and all the grammarians of ancient Rome. If anyone wants to see this proved, let him (as I have said once before) try to translate any school-divine into one of the modern languages—French, English, or any other ample language—since whatever cannot be made intelligible in most of these is not intelligible in the Latin either. This unintelligibility of language, though I cannot mark it down as false philosophy, does have one quality: not only to hide the truth, but also to make people think they have it, and so give up further searching.

Lastly, as for the errors brought in from false or uncertain history, what is the whole catalogue of fictitious miracles in the lives of the saints, and all the accounts of apparitions and departed spirits, alleged by the doctors of the Roman Church to support their doctrines of Hell and Purgatory, the power of exorcism, and other doctrines that have no warrant in either reason or Scripture? And what too of those traditions they call the unwritten word of God, but which are old wives' tales? Some bits of these can indeed be found scattered in the writings of the ancient Fathers, but those Fathers were people who could too easily believe false reports; and producing their opinions as testimony of the truth of what they believed has no greater force with those who (according to the counsel of 1 John 4:1) examine spirits, than this: in any matter touching the power of the Roman Church (the abuse of which they either did not suspect, or stood to benefit from), it discredits their testimony, by their too ready belief in such reports—since the most sincere people, without much knowledge of natural causes (as the Fathers were), are commonly the most prone to such credulity. The best people are naturally the least suspicious of fraudulent intentions. Pope Gregory and St. Bernard have something to say about apparitions of departed spirits who said they were in Purgatory, and our own Bede does as well; but nowhere, I believe, except by report from others. If they, or anyone else, were to relate such stories of their own direct knowledge, they would not thereby confirm such empty reports the more; they would only reveal their own weakness, or deception.

Along with the introduction of false philosophy, we may also include the suppression of true philosophy by those who, neither by lawful authority nor by sufficient study, are competent judges of the truth. Our own voyages make manifest, and all who are learned in the humane sciences now acknowledge, that there are antipodes; and every day it appears more and more that years and days are determined by motions of the earth. Nevertheless, people who have in their writings merely supposed such a doctrine as an occasion to set out the reasons for and against it have been punished for it by ecclesiastical authority. But what reason is there for this? Is it because such opinions are contrary to true religion? They cannot be, if they are true. Let the truth therefore first be examined by competent judges, or refuted by those who claim to know the contrary. Is it because they are contrary to the established religion? Then let them be silenced by the laws of those to whom the teachers of them are subject, that is, by the civil laws; for disobedience may lawfully be punished in those who teach even true philosophy against the laws. Is it because they tend toward disorder in government, by countenancing rebellion or sedition? Then let them be silenced, and the teachers punished, by virtue of his power to whom the care of the public peace is committed, which is the civil authority. For whatever power ecclesiastics take on themselves (in any place where they are subject to the state) in their own right, even if they call it God's right, is nothing but usurpation.
